Raise Against Evidence, Not Narrative

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 12 February 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

Investors price risk. Narrative asks them to imagine the risk away; evidence removes some of it. Even a small amount of real evidence changes which investors take the call, how fast they move and what they ask for. That matters more in 2026 than it did two years ago, because venture money is concentrating: rounds of $100 million or more took 87.5% of US venture dollars in the first half of the year, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by almost half.

Not investment or legal advice. lowob advises on narrative and readiness; it doesn't arrange, value or negotiate rounds.

Why evidence carries more weight in 2026

The headline numbers say venture is booming. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor recorded $515.8 billion of US deal value through the third quarter of 2026, with AI companies taking 82.7% of it. Crunchbase counted a record $510 billion invested globally in the first half alone.

Underneath, the market is narrow. PitchBook's second-quarter report found megadeals took 87.5% of the $412.7 billion deployed in the first half, and deals under $100 million fell to 12.5% of value, from 43.8% in 2024. One investor quoted in the report said he had never seen a more "haves and have-nots" market. Carta, which sees rounds raised on its own platform, found seed capital fell from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion between the first halves of 2025 and 2026, and seed round counts fell from 481 to 381 between the first quarters.

Datasets differ. PitchBook expects a record number of US first financings this year, while Carta sees fewer seed rounds. Both show the same thing for a founder outside the top tier: investors have more choice than founders do, and they choose the company that has already removed some risk.

What counts as evidence at each stage

StageEvidence investors weight mostUsually not enough on its own
Pre-seedFounder-market fit, a sharp problem, 5 to 10 named people who'd use itFollower counts, a waitlist nobody has been asked to act on
SeedDesign partners or pilots with usage, early retention, a few paying usersTestnet activity driven by points or airdrops
Series ARepeatable acquisition, revenue or fees that recur, a channel that scalesOne big logo with no expansion

In web3, the trap is activity that was paid for. Points programmes and incentive campaigns produce numbers that look like adoption until the incentive stops. Sophisticated investors now strip them out, so you should strip them out first and show what's left. Our piece on airdrops, points and community incentives covers how to separate the two.

In AI, the trap is the demo. A good demo proves the model can do something once. Investors want to see that a customer let it do the job every day.

The bar also rises with the price. Carta's median post-money valuation was $21.6 million at seed and $63 million at Series A in the first quarter of 2026. A Series A investor paying three times the seed price is buying proof that the seed-stage evidence repeated.

Building the evidence log

Keep one running document. Every entry is dated and specific.

  • Usage: who used it, how often, for what.
  • Quotes: what a user said, in their words, with permission to reuse.
  • Commitments: pilots, LOIs, integrations, partnerships with a named counterpart.
  • Community work: contributions, referrals, content made by people you didn't pay.
  • Losses: deals you lost and why. Investors trust a founder who knows why they lose.

Each entry works best as a small decision record: what happened, who was involved, the date and what it showed. The losses line follows the same discipline as win-loss analysis in a sales team, and it is the line founders most often leave blank.

The log has to last. Carta's first-quarter data puts the median gap between seed and Series A at two years. The log you start before the seed round is the one a Series A investor will read, so entries need dates, sources and enough context to be understood by someone who was not there.

This log is also your customer case-study source and your community recognition list. It's the first shared asset between the three workstreams from You don't have three problems.

One design partner using the product weekly is worth more than another month of deck revisions.

Rewriting the deck around it

Move your best evidence to slide 2 or 3, before the market slide. Then let the market slide answer the question the evidence raised: if this one buyer wants it, how many more are there?

Attention is short. DocSend's pitch deck index recorded investors spending an average of between 2 minutes 18 seconds and 2 minutes 30 seconds per deck in the weeks it reported across late 2023 and 2024. Evidence placed on slide 11 may never be read. Evidence on slide 2 sets the frame for everything after it.

The vision slide gets shorter. Evidence does the work vision was doing.

Deck positionNarrative-led deckEvidence-led deck
Slide 2The visionWhat a named user did with the product, with dates
Slide 3Market sizeThe pattern across users: retention, payment, referral
Market slideTop-down totalHow many more buyers look like the ones in slide 2
Vision slideThree slides of futureOne slide: what this round proves next

When you don't have any yet

Then the honest move is to raise less, from people who back founders at the idea stage, or to spend four to six weeks getting the first evidence before you go out. One design partner using the product weekly is worth more than another month of deck revisions. Our piece on making your first ten customers design partners sets out how to recruit them.

Market conditions reinforce the point. PitchBook found AI companies posted a median valuation step-up of 2.2x in 2026 against 1.6x for non-AI companies. The gap rewards companies whose evidence is already strong and penalises those still selling a story, in either category.

lowob takeaways

  • Evidence removes risk; narrative asks investors to ignore it. In a concentrated market, investors choose the company that has already removed some.
  • Strip out paid-for activity before an investor does. Points, airdrops and free tiers are acquisition cost, not demand.
  • Build the log to last two years. The median seed-to-Series A gap is two years, so date and source every entry.
  • Put the best evidence on slide 2 or 3. Investors spend minutes, not hours, on a deck.

Common questions

What evidence do investors want at seed stage?

Design partners or pilots with real usage, early retention and a few paying users. Testnet activity driven by points or airdrops, follower counts and untested waitlists are usually not enough on their own.

Where should traction go in a pitch deck?

On slide 2 or 3, before the market slide. Then let the market slide answer how many more buyers look like the ones you have. Investors spent an average of under two and a half minutes per deck in DocSend's 2023 to 2024 data.

What should I do if I have no traction before fundraising?

Raise less, from investors who back founders at the idea stage, or spend four to six weeks getting first evidence before going out. One design partner using the product weekly is worth more than another month of deck revisions.

Is it harder to raise a seed round in 2026?

For most companies, yes. Venture totals are at records, but megadeals took 87.5% of US venture dollars in the first half of 2026, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by almost half year on year.

Sources and notes

  • PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q3 2026, October 2026. US data through September 2026; figures taken from the NVCA summary page.
  • PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q2 2026, data as of 30 June 2026. US only; recent quarters are revised upward as deals are reported.
  • The Next Web, Megadeals took 87.5% of US venture dollars, 12 August 2026. News report on PitchBook valuation data; used for the AI and non-AI step-up figures.
  • Carta, State of Private Markets Q1 2026, 29 May 2026. Rounds raised by companies on Carta's platform, mostly US.
  • Carta, The venture market shifted in the first half of the year, 8 July 2026. Carta platform data; first half 2026 against first half 2025.
  • Crunchbase News, Global startup investment hit record $510B in H1 2026, 2 July 2026. Global data; totals include very large AI lab rounds.
  • DocSend, Pitch deck interest index, accessed November 2026. Vendor platform data; the time-per-deck figures date from 2023 and 2024.
